h: Vermeer, Moore and a famous film cameo
p: A few paintings deserve a special trip on their own. Vermeer's The Guitar Player is one of only a few dozen works by the Dutch master anywhere in the world, and Rembrandt's late self-portrait, with its mysterious circles in the background, is one of those pictures that seems to look right back at you. Take your time with both; the rooms are calm enough that you can.

Outside, the art carries on. Sculptures by big twentieth-century names, including Henry Moore and Barbara Hepworth, sit out in the landscape, so you can turn a walk around the grounds into a gentle hunt. Children often find this the best bit, as there's space to run between the pieces and no one shushing them.

Film fans might recognise the place, too. Kenwood famously appeared in Notting Hill, in the scene where Hugh Grant's character visits a period-drama film set, so expect a few knowing smiles from visitors of a certain age.

For a classic Kenwood day, aim for the morning in the house, a coffee or lunch at the café in the old service buildings, then an afternoon on the Heath. Parliament Hill, on the southern side, has one of the best free views across the London skyline, and the open-air bathing ponds are a much-loved local tradition for hardy swimmers. Highgate Cemetery is also within walking distance if you'd like something atmospheric to round things off.
Getting there is easiest by bus along Hampstead Lane or on foot across the Heath from Hampstead, Highgate or Gospel Oak stations, so wear shoes that can cope with a bit of mud.
